q: Do the paper's linear-in-p and 1/sqrt(N) scaling laws survive under CORRELATED (non-Markovian, spatially/temporally correlated) noise, or do they only hold for independent local depolarizing noise?
basis: Both this replication and the paper use uncorrelated local Pauli/depolarizing channels (or IBMQ's average-error device model). Real superconducting hardware exhibits correlated crosstalk and low-frequency 1/f drift that violates the standard Markovian assumption. The paper's linear-in-p slope prediction depends on the noise being local and independent per gate; correlated noise typically produces superlinear or non-monotone error growth (see Wallman & Emerson 2016; Blume-Kohout et al. 2022 on non-Markovian VQE bias).
next_steps: (1) Implement a Pauli-Lindblad correlated-noise model in Qiskit-Aer using the recent qiskit-ibm-runtime noise-learning primitives (free, open-source). (2) Rerun the same 3-point p-sweep with (a) uncorrelated depolarizing (baseline, already done), (b) Pauli-Lindblad correlated per pair of adjacent qubits, (c) same but with slow drift (T2* modulation). (3) Fit slope-in-p for each and report deviation from the linear law. (4) Cross-check against IBM's freely available Kyiv/Sherbrooke device noise-learning snapshots.

q: How much of the depolarizing-noise energy error (0.04-0.22 Ha) can be recovered by modern error-mitigation methods (ZNE, PEC, PEA) that were not available/mature at the time of the 2021 paper?
basis: Neither the paper nor this replication tested error mitigation, but the 2022-2025 literature (Kandala et al., Kim et al. 2023 Nature, van den Berg et al. 2023) shows ZNE and PEC can recover chemical accuracy at 1q errors 10^-3--10^-4. The paper's energy errors at p=10^-3 (~0.04 Ha) and p=10^-2 (~0.22 Ha) are well above chemical accuracy (1.6e-3 Ha); the open question is what fraction ZNE/PEC recovers for THIS specific ansatz and this specific Hamiltonian.
next_steps: (1) Rerun the p=1e-3 and p=1e-2 depolarizing cases with Qiskit's built-in ZNE (linear + Richardson extrapolation, folding factors [1,3,5]) using mitiq (open-source, free). (2) Add PEC via the Aer noise-model channel decomposition (analytic for depolarizing). (3) Report mitigated |E - E_noiseless| vs unmitigated. Predicted outcome: ZNE recovers p=1e-3 to within 5e-3 Ha; PEC to within 1e-3 Ha but at 10-100x sampling overhead.

q: Do the paper's conclusions transfer to strongly-correlated molecules (H2 chains, LiH, N2 stretched bond) where the ground state has substantial multireference character and depth-1 hardware-efficient ansatze demonstrably fail?
basis: H2/STO-3G is a 4-qubit weakly-correlated system where the depth-1 ansatz already gets within 20 mHa of FCI in the ideal limit; the noise-error study is on a benign landscape. For LiH/6-31G (12 qubits) or stretched H2 chains, the ideal-simulator error is 10-100 mHa and multireference character makes the SPSA optimizer landscape non-convex; noise-induced barren plateaus become dominant. The paper's scaling laws may not survive this qualitative regime change.
next_steps: (1) Build LiH/STO-3G (10 qubits, 631 JW Pauli terms) using the same PySCF+OpenFermion pipeline (already coded here). (2) Rerun the depolarizing sweep at p in {1e-4, 1e-3} with the same ansatz-family scaled to 10 qubits. (3) Test whether |delta E| still scales linearly in p or whether barren-plateau-induced flat optimizer landscape dominates. (4) Bonus: run a stretched H2 chain (H4 at R=1.5 Ang) which is the canonical multireference test bed. Expected free budget: ~2 hours CPU on m1 for LiH, ~10 hours for H4.

q: How transferable are the scaling laws across noise-model FAMILIES (depolarizing vs amplitude-damping vs coherent-rotation vs realistic T1/T2+gate-time IBMQ)? The paper conflates these under a single "noise" term but they have qualitatively different failure modes.
basis: Depolarizing noise is unbiased and symmetric across all Paulis, so its energy-error slope is close to n_gates * ||H||. Amplitude damping is biased toward |0> and produces systematic energy shifts even at low p. Coherent (over-rotation) errors do not average to zero and can produce non-monotone E(p). This replication tested only depolarizing; the paper tested IBMQ device noise (which mixes all three) as a black box. Whether the linear-in-p law holds separately for each channel family is unresolved.
next_steps: (1) Split the depolarizing sweep into three parallel sweeps: (a) pure amplitude-damping via Aer's amplitude_damping_error, (b) pure phase-damping via phase_damping_error, (c) pure coherent over-rotation via a Kraus channel implementing a small unitary error per gate. (2) Compare slope-in-p across the four channel families. (3) Report which channels satisfy monotonicity and which produce oscillatory E(p). (4) Fit a linear combination and check whether IBMQ device-noise energy error decomposes as a weighted sum of the individual channel contributions.

q: Can a machine-learning-selected error-mitigation strategy (choose ZNE vs PEC vs symmetry-verification vs Clifford-data-regression per-shot based on ansatz+Hamiltonian features) outperform any single mitigation method, and does that ML selector generalize across the paper's 12-ansatz family?
basis: The paper's C5 finding ("noise reshuffles the ranking of ansatze") plus modern QEM heterogeneity implies the optimal mitigation strategy also depends on ansatz structure. No published work systematically learns the (ansatz, noise, molecule) -> mitigation mapping. This is a natural extension question: if noise breaks ansatz ranking, does noise+mitigation restore it?
next_steps: (1) First reproduce C5: run the 12-ansatz sweep from the paper's Table I under the same p=1e-3 depolarizing model (~12x current wall time, ~1 hour). (2) For each ansatz, apply ZNE, PEC, and symmetry-verification (parity check on JW-mapped H2). (3) Train a simple gradient-boosted classifier (features: ansatz depth, 2q-gate count, entangling entropy at random init) to predict which mitigation minimizes |E - E_FCI|. (4) Cross-validate on LiH (question 3 above). Free endpoints: use CELS chicago-N via aggregator for the ML classifier training (sklearn is offline).
